question: What did the UK government announce in its November 2025 budget?
text:
Chancellor Rachel Reeves presented the UK’s **Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025**. Its biggest announcements were **scrapping the two-child limit on Universal Credit** and **extending the freeze on income tax and National Insurance thresholds to April 2031**. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated that the Budget’s tax measures would raise an additional **£26 billion in 2029–30**. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block))

| Area | What the government announced |
|---|---|
| **Benefits and pay** | The two-child limit would end in April 2026. The government estimated that this would leave 450,000 fewer children in poverty by 2029–30 than if the limit stayed. From April 2026, the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over would rise to **£12.71 an hour**, and the full new State Pension would rise by about **£575 a year**. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)) |
| **Income tax and savings** | Key tax thresholds would stay frozen until April 2031, so pay rises could push more people into tax or into higher bands even without an increase in the main rates on earnings. The ordinary and upper dividend tax rates would rise by **2 percentage points** from April 2026, with increases on savings and property income following in April 2027. The annual cash ISA limit for under-65s would fall to **£12,000** from April 2027, within the unchanged **£20,000** overall ISA allowance. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)) |
| **Pension contributions** | From April 2029, only the first **£2,000 a year** paid into a pension through salary sacrifice would remain exempt from employee and employer National Insurance. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)) |
| **Household bills** | Energy levy changes were expected to cut household energy bills in Great Britain by about **£150 on average** from April 2026. The government also announced a freeze on regulated rail fares in England. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)) |
| **Property, motoring and business** | From April 2028, England would get an annual council tax surcharge of **£2,500 to £7,500** on homes valued at **£2 million or more**, and electric and plug-in hybrid cars would face a new mileage-based charge. The Budget also extended the temporary **5p fuel duty cut** through August 2026 and set lower business rates for eligible retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10405/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)) |

The OBR’s forecast at the time was for real GDP growth to average **1.5%** over the following five years, down from **1.8%** in its March forecast. It projected that the government would meet its rule for day-to-day spending with a **£22 billion margin in 2029–30**. ([obr.uk](https://obr.uk/efo/economic-and-fiscal-outlook-november-2025/?utm_source=openai))
